questions.q: Why should a stakeholder presentation open with the recommendation instead of the data and method?
options: Business audiences decide on the answer and the evidence, so leading with the ask focuses the discussion and leaves the method for the appendix
It hides the method from reviewers
Recommendations do not need evidence
The order of slides does not matter
questions.explain: Technical work is ordered by how you did it; decisions are ordered by what the audience must decide. Answer first, evidence second, method last.

questions.q: Why did the deck use cross-validated predictions over all 3,690 customers for the headline precision, alongside the test set result?
options: Cross-validation is always more accurate than a test set
Because the test set was corrupted
The top 10% of the test set is only 74 customers, while the cross-validated top 10% is the full 369 the team can contact, with a tighter interval
Because the model was trained on all customers
questions.explain: Each cross-validated prediction comes from a model that never saw that customer, and the top decile is the real contact-list size. The test result (0.405) and the pooled result (0.401) agree.

questions.q: The sensitivity table shows the program loses money if the offer saves fewer than about 16% of would-be churners. What does that tell the stakeholder?
options: The model is inaccurate
The value depends on an assumed save rate that the model cannot supply, so a pilot with a randomized holdout should measure it
The program should be cancelled
The break-even precision is wrong
questions.explain: The model ranks churn risk; whether an offer changes behavior is a separate question. The honest recommendation is to test the offer, not assume it works.

questions.q: In the deck, the model's top decile churns at 40.1% (95% CI 35.0% to 45.0%) against a 20.8% break-even. Why is this a strong statement?
options: Because 40% is a round number
Because the whole interval sits above the break-even, so even a pessimistic reading of the precision still pays under the stated assumptions
Because intervals are not needed
Because the break-even is measured on the test set
questions.explain: Showing that the lower end of the interval clears the break-even addresses the question 'how sure are you?' with numbers rather than reassurance.

questions.q: Which is the best way to present limitations?
options: Omit them so the recommendation is not weakened
Mention that 'there are always some caveats'
Move them to the end of the appendix in small type
State them specifically, such as one snapshot, an assumed save rate below which the program loses money, and a modest signal (six in ten flagged customers would not have left)
questions.explain: Specific limitations build trust because they show you know exactly where the work is weak. Vague ones sound evasive.
